newsitem.title: USA: Conn. atty general backs 20 pct electric rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Conn. atty general backs 20 pct electric rate cut.

text.p: Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal urged lawmakers on Thursday to adopt an electricity deregulation plan that would slash rates by up to 20 percent for all users.
But top utility company officials voiced strong opposition to the state's draft bill on deregulation in testimony before the Energy and Technology Committee .
United Illuminating Co Chief Executive Richard Grossi called the draft bill, which proposes full deregulation by 2000, "a recipe for disaster."
Instead, Grossi urged an "orderly transition period" beginning in 1999 and phased in over five years.
The Attorney General told reporters his deregulation goal all along has been to see competition by July 1998.
"The bill now speaks of the year 2000," he said. "If it takes an additional 18 months, I don't think that is tragic, but I do think that we can have real, lasting, fundamental change by 1998."
"We ought not to settle lightly for postponements... There ought to be full competition by the year 2000, if not 1998."
He said he was "tremendously encouraged" that even United Illuminating and Northeast Utilities "accept the fact that change is inevitable."
"The utilities naturally want delay," he said.

"But I don't think we can afford it. That time is critical to consumers and our economy. I think that this legislature will adopt the principles of restructuring and competition on a much more accelerated timetable."
"UI is not opposed to competition -- we simply want it done right" was the way Grossi put it, adding the legislative focus should be competitive prices for all electric users.

Northeast Utilities' chief financial officer John Forsgren noted the "significant impact (deregulation will have on CP&L's) 6,000 Connecticut employees and the more than one million Connecticut custmers in 149 communities we serve, including the $150 million we pay in state taxes and $60 million we pay in municipal property taxes, and the 80,000 Connecticut shareholders who have invested in the company."
He said NU plans "to be a major player in that competitive energy industry" which will be created by restructuring.
Both officials expressed concern about how the draft before the Connecticut legislature treats stranded costs.

Grossi argued UI should have the opportunity to recover 100 percent of all costs incurred to meet public service obligations, rather than the bill's allowance of 75 percent recovery of costs through rates.
The hearing marked the formal opening of debate in this legislative session over deregulation of Connecticut's $3 billion electric industry.
Republican Governor John Rowland testified Thursday that deregulation could "help make energy technology a major engine for Connecticut's economic development."

"Advanced gas turbines, derived from the latest aircraft engines produced by (Hartford-based) United Technologies, have a vast potential market for power generation applications, not just in this state but throughout the nation and the world," Rowland said.
Democrat Blumenthal said in his testimony that Connecticut citizens and businesses could not afford "exorbitant" rates which are currently about 35 percent higher than the national average.
He told reporters a 20 percent rate cut was "a realistic goal.

"Ten percent certainly is achieveable, and it ought to be possible using more generators, the existing transmission lines, but simply providing more options, more choices, and preserving safety in the environment."
The state's residents deserved "dramatically lower rates," he continued, adding: "Failure to move now with this plan will make Connecticut first in cost and last in competition."
